tagline: Southern Pines and the longleaf forest saved at Weymouth Woods
intro: East Connecticut Avenue is included in North Carolina’s scenic-byway guide. Southern Pines lies in the Sandhills, where longleaf pines once supplied timber, ships’ masts and resin for naval stores.

Railroads arrived in the Sandhills in the 1870s, followed by large-scale logging. Logging and naval stores operations had removed most of the original longleaf growth by 1900. Early in the twentieth century, author James Boyd’s grandfather bought land east of Southern Pines to protect its pines from logging.

Southern Pines developed as a winter health resort for Northerners. The James Boyd House, also called Weymouth, is a Colonial Revival brick home built in the 1920s. Nearby Weymouth Woods preserves longleaf forest; Katharine Boyd’s 1963 land donation established the first natural area in the state parks system.

moments.title: Southern Pines
moments.text: Southern Pines began with plans for a winter health resort for Northerners: land was purchased in 1884, and incorporation followed in 1887. By 1898, African Americans were barred from living or doing business in the town. The historic district developed between 1883 and 1940, leaving examples of Queen Anne, Colonial Revival and Craftsman architecture. Its buildings include the passenger depot, the 1917 Arcade Building, the 1937 post office and the 1939 public library. The passenger station was built in 1898 by a predecessor of the Seaboard Air Line Railroad. Renovated in 1948, it was restored to that design in 2004.

moments.title: James Boyd House
moments.text: Weymouth, the James Boyd House, has housed the Weymouth Center for the Arts and Humanities since 1979. Historical novelist James Boyd built the house after World War I, with a design by architect Aymar Embury II. The brick Colonial Revival dwelling has a two-story central block joined to wings by two-story connecting sections. The house entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1977, two years before the arts center made its home here.

moments.title: Weymouth Woods
moments.text: Older pines at Weymouth Woods bear scars from the naval stores industry. Workers collected resin from elongated, inverted V-shaped cuts in the trunks and distilled it into turpentine. James Boyd’s grandfather bought land to save the longleaf pines from logging and named the estate Weymouth for trees it recalled in England. In 1963, Katharine Boyd donated 403 acres to the state. The preserve’s exhibit hall explains the longleaf forest, prescribed fire and the earlier uses of pine resin. James Creek bisects the preserve, with dark, tannin-stained water characteristic of a blackwater creek.
moments.notice: Older pines bear scars left by resin harvesting.
